learning_objective: The learner will classify eight classroom scenarios as constructivism, social constructivism, constructionism, or social constructionism, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** which-learning-theory
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Understand
**Bloom Verb:** classify
**Learning Objective:** The learner will classify eight classroom scenarios as constructivism, social constructivism, constructionism, or social constructionism, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt. **Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/automating-instructional-design/tree/main/docs/sims/zpd-visualization
**Prerequisites:** constructivism, social constructivism, zone of proximal development, constructionism, social constructionism (all defined in the section "How Students Learn: Four Theories" above). **Evidence of Mastery:** The learner places each of 8 scenarios in one of four theory bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct theory" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the definitions is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Constructivism and constructionism are the same. (2) Any group activity is social constructivism. (3) Building something alone is not learning by building. **Instructional Rationale:** Classifying scenarios requires finding each theory's defining feature: building from prior knowledge, learning with a more capable helper, making an artifact, or making an artifact as a team. The pairs of near scenarios force attention to the defining feature. **Content:** Four bins with definitions shown on request: | Theory | Definition shown | |---|---| | Constructivism | A learner builds new understanding by connecting it to what they already know and revising their own ideas | | Social constructivism | A learner builds understanding through interaction with others who can help, within reach of what they can do alone | | Constructionism | A learner learns especially well by making a tangible, shareable artifact | | Social constructionism | A group learns by building a shared artifact together | Eight scenarios: | # | Scenario shown to the learner | Correct theory | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | A student changes her idea that heavier objects fall faster after a ball-drop experiment contradicts it. | Constructivism | She revises her own understanding in light of experience. | | 2 | A student cannot solve a proportion problem alone, solves it after a classmate asks "what is the total, and what is the count?" | Social constructivism | A peer's help lets her do something just beyond what she can do alone. | | 3 | A student builds a working catapult, tests it, and redesigns the arm to fly farther. | Constructionism | The learning comes from making and improving a tangible artifact. | | 4 | A team of four builds a food-waste dashboard, argues about its design, and presents it to the cafeteria staff. | Social constructionism | The group builds a shared artifact together. | | 5 | A student tries to explain a wrong idea about fractions, sees a fraction-bar model contradict it, and rebuilds the idea. | Constructivism | The student revises an existing idea. | | 6 | A teacher gives a hint and then withdraws it as the student begins to solve similar problems alone. | Social constructivism | Temporary help in the student's zone of proximal development is removed as the student gains skill. | | 7 | A student programs a small game alone and finds a bug by playing it. | Constructionism | The student learns by making an artifact alone. | | 8 | A class builds a mural about the school's history, deciding together what to include. | Social constructionism | The group builds a shared artifact together. | **Provenance:** Definitions follow the chapter section "How Students Learn: Four Theories." The scenarios are illustrative, written for this chapter. **Rules:** Each scenario has exactly one correct theory, given in Content. A scenario is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees one scenario at a time and the four theories. 2. The learner places the scenario and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text. 3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct theory and reason are shown. 4. After all 8 scenarios, the sim shows the score and lists misplaced scenarios with their correct theories. 5. The learner should notice that scenarios 3 and 4 both involve building, and differ only in whether the building is done by one student or a team. **Feedback:** 8 scenarios, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [theory]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the theory]." After the second attempt the correct theory is revealed and the scenario counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can tell the four theories apart." For a score < 7: "Review the four definitions and try again; the scenarios will be reshuffled." **Starting State:** Scenario 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the four bins, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "Which learning theory does this show?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter defines four theories (constructivism, social constructivism, constructionism, social constructionism) and uses the food-waste dashboard as the social constructionism example. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.
